title: Dharma, Karma, Samsara, Moksha
bigQuestion: What big ideas do Hindu texts teach about how to live, and how do stories help people remember them?

story.title: Every Action Is a Seed
story.kicker: A girl plants a seed, and her grandfather tells her what his teachers told him.
paragraphs: Meera kneels in her grandfather's backyard in Naperville. It is May, and the soil is cool. She pushes a bean seed into the dirt with one finger. Then she pats the soil flat and pours water from a small green can.

Her grandfather, Dada, watches from a lawn chair. "Do you know what my teachers said in India?" he asks. "They said every action is a seed too. A kind action grows into something. So does an unkind one." Meera looks at the wet soil. "Even little things?" she asks.

Dada nods. "That idea is called karma," he says. "Many Hindus believe our actions have results, now or later. Some believe the results can reach into another life." He tells her the Gita says to do your work well without worrying about the prize.

Meera thinks about the bean. She cannot see it now, but she knows it is there. She decides to water it every morning. "Then I will plant good seeds," she says. Dada smiles. "That is how my mother taught it to me," he says. "With a garden."
story.think: Why do you think Dada used a seed to explain karma? What other picture could help someone understand an idea like this?

lessons.title: Dharma: The Right Way to Live
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus use the word dharma for duty and the right way to live, and it can be different for each person.
reading: In the Ramayana, Prince Rama is told he must leave home for fourteen years. He could argue. Instead, he goes, because he wants to keep his father's promise. Many Hindus see Rama as a model of *dharma*.

Dharma is a Sanskrit word. It means duty, what is right, and the order that holds life together. Hindus believe dharma is not the same for everyone. A student, a parent and a ruler each have their own duties.

Hindu texts give many examples of dharma. Some are clear, like telling the truth and not hurting others. Some are hard. In the Mahabharata, good people argue about what dharma asks. The texts show that finding the right thing can take careful thought.

words.d: duty, what is right, and the right way to live; a key word in Hindu texts
the old language of India in which the Vedas, epics and many Hindu texts were written

look.title: Three People, Three Duties
look.text: A student studies hard and respects her teacher. A father works to feed his family. A king protects his people and rules fairly. Hindu texts say each of these people is following dharma.
look.prompt: Why might dharma look different for a student, a father and a king? What is one duty you have at school?

check.q: What does the word dharma mean?
choices: Duty and the right way to live
check.why: Dharma means duty, what is right and the right way to live. Freedom from rebirth is moksha.

check.q: Why do many Hindus see Rama as a model of dharma?
choices: He left home to keep his father's promise
He built a temple in Lemont
check.why: In the Ramayana, Rama goes to the forest to keep his father's word, so many Hindus honor him as a model of dharma.

check.q: What do Hindu texts say about dharma for different people?
choices: It is exactly the same for everyone
Each person's duties can be different
check.why: Hindu texts teach that a student, a parent and a ruler each have their own duties.

lessons.title: Karma: Actions Have Results
lessons.mainIdea: Karma means action, and Hindus believe every action has results.
reading: Think of Meera's bean seed. She plants it now, and it grows later. Many Hindus explain *karma* the same way. The word karma means action. Hindus believe good actions bring good results and harmful actions bring harmful ones.

Hindus believe the results of karma can come soon or much later. Many believe they can even come in a future life. This is why many Hindu families teach children to be kind, honest and careful in small things as well as big ones.

The Bhagavad Gita adds another idea. In it, Krishna tells Arjuna to do his duty but not to be greedy for the reward. Many readers take this to mean: do good work because it is right, not only for a prize. Scholars call this idea acting without attachment.

words.d: action; Hindus believe every action has results that come back to the one who acts
a famous Hindu text, part of the Mahabharata, in which Krishna teaches Arjuna

look.title: Work Without Greed for the Prize
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna: you have a right to do your work, but not to its results. Do not let the reward be your reason, and do not stop working either.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, retold in simple words (based on K.T. Telang's translation, 1882)
look.prompt: What does Krishna tell Arjuna to care about: the work or the prize? Say it in your own words.

check.q: What does the word karma mean?
check.why: Karma means action. Hindus believe actions have results.

check.q: In the Gita, what does Krishna tell Arjuna about his work?
choices: Work only when you get a prize
Do your duty without being greedy for the reward
check.why: In Bhagavad Gita 2.47, Krishna tells Arjuna to act without making the reward his reason.

check.q: When do many Hindus believe the results of karma can come?
choices: Soon, later, or even in a future life
check.why: Hindus believe karma's results can come soon or later, and many believe even in another life.

lessons.title: Four Aims of Life
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu texts name four aims of a good life: dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
reading: Hindu texts say a full life has four aims. They are called the purusharthas. The first is dharma, doing what is right. The second is *artha*, earning a living and caring for a home. The third is *kama*, enjoying good things like music, food and love.

The fourth aim is moksha. Many Hindus believe it is freedom from the cycle of rebirth. The texts say the first three aims are good, but they should follow dharma. You should earn money honestly, for example, and enjoy life without hurting others.

The four aims show that Hindu texts do not ask everyone to give up the world. Many people work, raise families and celebrate festivals. The texts describe all of these as part of a good life when they are guided by dharma.

words.d: wealth and a good living; one of the four aims of life in Hindu texts
enjoyment and love; one of the four aims of life in Hindu texts
the four aims of life in Hindu texts: dharma, artha, kama and moksha

look.title: The Four Aims
look.unit: order in which texts list them
look.cite: The four purusharthas as listed in the Mahabharata and later Hindu texts
look.prompt: Which aim do the texts say should guide the other three?

check.q: Which aim is about earning a living?
check.why: Artha means wealth and a good living, one of the four aims.

check.q: What do the texts say should guide wealth and enjoyment?
check.why: Hindu texts teach that artha and kama should follow dharma.

check.q: What do the four aims show?
choices: Work, family and joy can be part of a good life
check.why: The four aims include earning and enjoyment, guided by dharma, as parts of a good life.

lessons.title: Samsara: The Wheel of Rebirth
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe in samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth.
reading: In the Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna a picture. A person takes off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones. Krishna says the self does the same with bodies. Many Hindus read this verse as a teaching about rebirth.

The belief in rebirth is called *samsara*. Samsara means wandering or flowing on. Many Hindus believe the self is born, dies and is born again, many times. They believe karma helps shape each new life.

Samsara is often pictured as a wheel that keeps turning. Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs also speak of rebirth, in their own ways. Hindu schools explain samsara differently, but many share this picture of a long journey through many lives.

words.d: the cycle of birth, death and rebirth that many Hindus believe in
being born again in a new body after death, as many Hindus believe

look.title: New Clothes
look.text: Krishna says: just as a person takes off old clothes and puts on new ones, the self in the body leaves old bodies and enters new ones.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22, retold in simple words (based on K.T. Telang's translation, Sacred Books of the East 8, 1882)
look.prompt: What is compared to clothes in this verse? What is compared to the person wearing them?

check.q: What is samsara?
choices: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth
check.why: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth many Hindus believe in.

check.q: In Gita 2.22, what does the self set aside like old clothes?
check.why: The Gita compares bodies to clothes that are set aside for new ones.

check.q: Which other traditions also speak of rebirth?
check.why: Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs also speak of rebirth, each in their own way.

lessons.title: Moksha: Freedom
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the highest goal is moksha, freedom from the cycle of rebirth.
reading: Picture a bird in a cage. The door opens, and the bird flies free. Some Hindu teachers use pictures like this to describe *moksha*. Moksha means freedom or release.

Many Hindus believe moksha is freedom from samsara, the cycle of rebirth. They describe it as deep peace. Different Hindu schools describe it in different ways. Some say the self finds it is one with ultimate reality. Others say the soul lives forever in loving closeness to God.
Hindu texts give several ways to seek moksha. Some teach knowledge, some teach selfless action, and some teach loving devotion. You will learn about these three paths later in this chapter.

words.d: freedom or release; many Hindus believe it is freedom from the cycle of rebirth
being set free; another word used for moksha

look.title: Two Ways to Describe Freedom
look.text: One Hindu teacher says moksha is like a drop of water joining the ocean. Another says it is like a child resting safe in a parent's arms, still a child, but never apart again.
look.prompt: How are these two pictures of moksha alike? How are they different?

check.q: What does moksha mean?
check.why: Moksha means freedom or release, which many Hindus believe is freedom from rebirth.

check.q: From what do many Hindus believe moksha frees a person?
check.why: Many Hindus believe moksha is freedom from samsara, the cycle of rebirth.

check.q: Do all Hindu schools describe moksha the same way?
choices: No, they describe it in different ways
check.why: Some schools speak of oneness with ultimate reality and others of loving closeness to God.

lessons.title: Karma in a Story You Know
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu stories often show how actions lead to results, which helps readers remember karma.
reading: Remember the Ramayana. When Rama is in the forest, a bird named Jatayu tries to save Sita from Ravana. Jatayu is badly hurt. Rama later honors the brave bird with care and funeral rites. Many readers see Jatayu's brave act as good karma.
Ravana's story shows the other side. He takes Sita away by force. In the end he loses his kingdom and his life. Many Hindu tellers use Ravana to show that harmful actions bring harmful results.

Stories like these helped families teach karma long before most children could read. A grandmother telling the Ramayana could point to each character and ask, what did this action lead to? Many families still teach this way today.

words.d: the Hindu epic about Prince Rama, his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana
the brave vulture in the Ramayana who tries to save Sita

look.title: Follow the Action
look.text: Hanuman leaps across the sea to find Sita. He brings her Rama's ring and tells her help is coming. Sita feels hope again.
look.prompt: What action did Hanuman take? What result came from it? How might a Hindu storyteller use this to teach karma?

check.q: Who tries to save Sita and is hurt by Ravana?
check.why: In the Ramayana, the vulture Jatayu tries to stop Ravana and is badly hurt.

check.q: How do many tellers use Ravana's story?
choices: To show that harmful actions bring harmful results
To teach about the four Vedas
To describe the temple in Lemont
check.why: Many tellers use Ravana to show that harmful actions lead to harmful results.

check.q: Why did stories help families teach karma?
choices: Children could learn ideas before they could read
check.why: Families told stories like the Ramayana so children could learn karma by hearing them.

lessons.title: Brahman: One Reality, Many Forms
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus speak of one ultimate reality, Brahman, honored in many forms such as Vishnu, Shiva and Devi.
reading: Walk into a Hindu temple and you may see many murtis, or sacred images. There may be Vishnu, Shiva, Devi the Goddess, Ganesha and Hanuman. A visitor may wonder how one religion honors so many.

Many Hindus explain it this way. They speak of one ultimate reality called *Brahman*. They believe Brahman can be known through many forms. A very old verse of the Rig Veda says the wise call the one by many names (Rig Veda 1.164.46).

Hindus show this idea in different ways. Vaishnavas honor Vishnu as the Supreme. Shaivas honor Shiva. Shaktas honor Devi, the Goddess. Many families honor several forms at one home shrine. These traditions are all part of Hinduism.

words.d: the one ultimate reality that many Hindus believe is behind everything
a sacred image of a deity, honored in temples and homes
a Hindu who honors Vishnu (often as Rama or Krishna) as the Supreme

look.title: Many Names
look.text: They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni... To what is One, sages give many a title.
look.cite: Rig Veda 1.164.46, Ralph T.H. Griffith, Hymns of the Rigveda (1896), shortened
look.prompt: What does this verse say about names? How do many Hindus use it to explain many forms?

check.q: What do many Hindus call the one ultimate reality?
check.why: Many Hindus speak of Brahman, the one ultimate reality.

check.q: Who do Shaivas honor as the Supreme?
check.why: Shaivas honor Shiva as the Supreme. Vaishnavas honor Vishnu.

check.q: What is a murti?
choices: A sacred image of a deity
check.why: A murti is a sacred image honored in temples and homes.

lessons.title: Three Paths
lessons.mainIdea: The Bhagavad Gita describes several paths toward moksha: action, knowledge and devotion.
reading: Picture three hikers climbing one mountain. One takes a steep path, one a winding path, one a path through the woods. Many Hindus use pictures like this for the paths the Gita describes.

The Gita names *karma yoga*, the path of selfless action. It names jnana yoga, the path of knowledge and wisdom. It also names *bhakti*, the path of loving devotion to God. Yoga here means a path or discipline, not only exercise.

Different Hindus stress different paths. Some teachers say knowledge matters most. Many devotional groups say bhakti is the heart of it all. Many readers say the paths work together, like strands in one rope.

words.d: the path of selfless action, doing one's duty without greed for reward
the path of knowledge and wisdom
loving devotion to God; a path described in the Bhagavad Gita

look.title: Paths in the Gita
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita chapters 2, 3 and 12, as commonly summarized by scholars
look.prompt: Which chapter of the Gita is known for teaching about devotion?

check.q: Which path is loving devotion to God?
check.why: Bhakti is the path of loving devotion described in the Gita.

check.q: What does karma yoga mean?
check.why: Karma yoga is doing one's duty without greed for the reward.

check.q: How do many readers see the three paths?
choices: As working together, like strands in one rope
check.why: Many readers say the paths of action, knowledge and devotion work together.

lessons.title: Putting the Ideas Together
lessons.mainIdea: Dharma, karma, samsara and moksha fit together as one picture of life in many Hindu texts.
reading: Think back to Meera's garden. Dharma is like knowing how to care for the plant. Karma is like the seeds she plants each day. Samsara is like the seasons that keep coming back.

Moksha, in this picture, is harder to show. Some Hindu teachers say it is like the gardener no longer needing the garden at all. Others say it is like resting forever with the one who made the garden. Hindus describe it in many ways.

Many Hindus say these ideas are not just for thinking. They shape daily choices, like being honest, helping at home and praying at a home shrine. Learning the words helps you understand what Hindu classmates and neighbors may mean.

words.d: duty and the right way to live
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth many Hindus believe in

look.title: Match the Picture
look.text: Seeds planted each day. Seasons that return again and again. Knowing how to care for a plant. A gate that opens out of the garden.
look.prompt: Match each picture to one idea: dharma, karma, samsara or moksha. Explain one match.

check.q: In the garden picture, which idea is like seasons that keep coming back?
check.why: Samsara, the cycle of rebirth, is like seasons that return.

check.q: In the garden picture, which idea is like seeds planted each day?
check.why: Karma is action, like seeds that grow into results.

check.q: What do many Hindus say these ideas shape?
choices: Daily choices like honesty and helping
check.why: Many Hindus say these ideas guide everyday choices.

review.q: Which word means duty and the right way to live?
review.why: Dharma means duty and what is right.

review.q: What do Hindus believe about karma?
review.why: Karma means action, and Hindus believe actions have results.

review.q: Which idea is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth?
review.why: Samsara is the cycle of rebirth.

review.q: Which is one of the four aims of life?
review.why: Artha, a good living, is one of the four aims, with dharma, kama and moksha.

review.q: Which text has Krishna teach Arjuna to work without greed for reward?
review.why: Krishna teaches Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita, 2.47.

review.q: Who do Shaktas honor as the Supreme?
The Gita compares changing bodies to what?
review.why: Gita 2.22 compares bodies to worn-out clothes set aside for new ones.
Moksha means freedom, which many Hindus believe is freedom from rebirth.
